en: There is nothing unknown to him; the entire realm of afflictions has come to its dissolution.
His compassion for friends, enemies, and others who are in distress never reaches exhaustion.
And when meditated upon, he removes the fear of living beings, just as the wind disperses a heap of cotton.
I bow to him by whom that Puṣpaketu was conquered and sent back to his own home. 7.1.1
He who is peaceful and free from conceptual proliferation, pure as a mass of snow, untainted by worldly dharmas,
and who is perceived at all times by those of well-disciplined minds through their application to ethical conduct and the other perfections;
he who is to be personally realized within, and who, like a fever or poison, has abandoned all undesirable views.
I pay homage to that Noble Dharma, which is the sole refuge for those whose passions have been removed. 7.1.2
That which consists of the states of those in training and those beyond training, belonging to the sages who observe vows and restraints—that is [faith].
It is faith... [the clarity of mind].
I bow to that noble Saṅgha, which is ever intent upon conquering the mind-born god [of desire]. || 7.1.3 ||
It would be better for one who fears the next world to rub out his eye with a glowing iron probe than to look [at such things] with a corrupted memory.
Women with restless eyes engage in idle chatter. || 7.1.4 ||
By means of smiles, amorous gestures, bashfulness, and fear; by turning away, by side-long glances, by words, by quarrels born of jealousy, and by playful dalliance.
Indeed, women are a bond through all states of being.
Whether standing, seated, lying down, turned away, well-adorned, or even unadorned— a woman, when being gazed upon, [overcomes] one who is very weak.
Even when depicted in a painting, she brings a man under her power.
It is better to fight with those who wield sharpened weapons—
[than with those who do not].
And women [corrupt] the intellect with their playful charms and their glances. || 7.1.7 ||
A wise person should not gaze at young women, nor should he speak to them; having observed them according to their age, he should regard them with the perception of a daughter or a sister.
Or, if passion should arise, he should reflect upon the impurity of the body.
He was fickle toward sense-objects—[the rest of the verse is missing]. || 7.1.8 ||
Rivers and women possess a similar power;
their banks and families are alike.
For rivers with their waters and faults cast down both riverbanks and noble families, even as women do.
Even a burning fire can be grasped;
even the bodiless wind can be grasped;
even an enraged serpent can be grasped.
But the minds of women cannot be restrained. || 7.1.10 ||
Women strike without distinction, taking no account of physical form, wealth, lineage, intellect, or prowess.
Like rivers crowded with flocks of water-birds. || 7.1.11 ||
They were like poisonous creepers that have been touched, like caves containing serpents that have been disturbed,
or like drawn swords that have been grasped.
For women indeed end in calamity. || 7.1.12 ||
Women who are intoxicated bestow intoxication,
while women who are free from intoxication bestow fear;
if they bring about both vice and fear, how can they be trusted?
How indeed are they worthy of being cultivated? 7.1.13
That kinsmen are divided by their own kin,
and friends likewise by their friends,
is due to those rogues who are experts at observing the faults of others.
Unnoble women strike back. || 7.1.14 ||
A woman remembers neither sweet words nor endearments, neither what has been done for her nor her own friendship;
a woman is as fickle as the forest fire itself.
It does not remain steady, like lightning among the clouds. || 7.1.15 ||
When they do not give, they become devoid of pride;
when they give, they fall into confusion; and toward those who bow before them, they become arrogant.
And women are more arrogant toward those who are proud. || 7.1.16 ||
They behave like masters toward those with virtues, but they behave like enemies toward those devoid of virtues;
they behave out of greed toward those who possess wealth.
They move about with contempt toward those who are destitute of wealth. || 7.1.17 ||
It is said that Senajit’s daughter desired a dog-cooker (outcaste),
Kumudvatī a fish-eater,
and Bṛhadrathā a lion.
For women, there is no place they cannot go. || 7.1.18 ||
They captivate with their lovely speech,
yet they strike with a sharpened mind;
honey remains upon the tongues of women.
In the heart lies the great poison, Hālāhala.
It would be better to take refuge in a cave inhabited by serpents, or a river teeming with crocodiles,
or a flowering creeper born of the forest, or a patch of ground with blazing fire;
for a woman is not a cave in a mountain, nor a river, nor a poisonous creeper, nor a terrifying, flaming wasteland.
For women have hearts like venomous serpents, crocodiles, poison, and fire; indeed, they are a sharp weapon.
"You are my source of joy, you alone are my heart, you are my refuge, you are my beloved; at the time of my end, my final goal is you—you are my supreme deity.
When young women speak in this manner, the wise should not praise them.
In the speech of women there is nectar born, yet in their very nature there is poison. || 7.1.21 ||
Just as you avoid a flowering creeper when it is infested by venomous snakes,
and just as you do not cross a river even when it has a good ford if it contains fierce crocodiles;
in that same way, recognizing a woman for what she is, abandon her even if she is virtuous and pleasing to the eye.
For all sense objects, though they come as pleasures, inevitably result in calamity.
This world wanders aimlessly, confined within the prison of existence; yet, apart from hearing this [teaching],
there is no bolt to shut the door of the house of miserable rebirths.
"Listen to the words of the sage, having first composed your minds. (7.1.23) Thus it is said.

§1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Kuśinagarī, in the vicinity of the Mallas, in the Śāla Grove of the Twin Trees. Then the Venerable Ānanda, at that very moment and at the time of the final nirvāṇa, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

"§2 How, venerable sir, should we conduct ourselves toward women after the passing of the Blessed One? By not looking at them, Ānanda; if one must look, by not conversing with them; and if one must converse, by maintaining mindfulness."

"Ānanda, I do not see even a single form that is so alluring, intoxicating, desirable, affection-inspiring, lovely, enticing, infatuating, binding, yearning-inducing, and fettering as the female form is for a man. A man, being impassioned, attached, greedy, fettered, infatuated, obsessed, and fallen into obsession with the female form—failing to see the danger and not discerning the escape—is under the sway of the female form."

“Ānanda, I do not perceive even a single sound, odor, taste, or tangible object that is so alluring, intoxicating, desirable, affection-inspiring, lovely, enticing, delusive, binding, yearning-arousing, or fettering as the touch of a woman to a man.

A man who is attached, bound, greedy, entangled, infatuated, obsessed, and fallen into a state of resolve regarding the touch of a woman—failing to see the danger and failing to discern the escape—is under the sway of the touch of a woman.”

§5. Ānanda, that which those who speak correctly would call "the universal snare," namely the bond of Māra, is women; this is what one should say when speaking correctly of a man's [bond]. For what reason? Because a woman, whether she is walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or reclining; whether awake, dancing, singing, playing an instrument, weeping, or laughing; whether well-dressed or poorly dressed; whether afflicted by illness or even dead—she remains having completely seized the mind of a man.

§6 Once upon a time, Ānanda, a certain man went to a cremation ground for some business or other. There he heard that a woman named so-and-so had been burned in such-and-such a place. Upon hearing this, he fainted and fell down right there.
The Blessed One said this; having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke further as follows.
One might converse with one who holds a sword in hand, or even converse with a female demon;
one might even seize a venomous serpent by which, once bitten, one does not live. || 1 ||
But he should never converse alone with a single woman;
for they bind one whose mindfulness is lost by means of glances, smiles, and gestures. (2)
Or rather, even with pleasant speech or difficult consolation, this person—[already] dead—is not [revived], for he is of the nature of disease. (3)

And this was said by the Blessed One, the Arhat: "O monks, there are these five dangers in a black snake. What are the five? It is prone to anger, it harbors resentment, it is treacherous, it is ungrateful, and its venom is sharp. In exactly the same way, O monks, there are these five dangers in a woman. What are the five? She is prone to anger, she harbors resentment, she is treacherous, she is ungrateful, and her venom is sharp. In this regard, the 'sharp venom' of a woman is that, for the most part, a woman possesses intense passion."

He who, once released from bondage, grieves for it; or he who, having encountered great calamity, laments it; or he who, having recovered from illness, broods over his former health—he is like one who pines for a woman long past.
For here, women are indeed the supreme bondage, a great affliction consisting of calamity, and a disease of the world;
therefore, if you have fallen into this state regarding a woman—
Surely your Kali age has departed, consisting as it did of youthful women.
The speech of women— whether it be "affectionate" or "pleasing"— should not be accepted by you;
for such is the nature born of women.
Honey on the tongue, poison in the heart.
Like rivers infested with crocodiles, like golden caves containing sleeping tigers,
women are both sweet and treacherous.
They are both delightful and flawed. 7.3.4.
They destroy the affection between brothers, mothers, sons, and friends; they bring disgrace upon the family; they produce passion and ignorance;
they are enemies to virtue, purity, and fortitude; they are snares for human beings.
Surely you do not understand women, which is why you are attached to them.
A woman takes no account of wealth, nor learning, nor physical beauty, nor noble lineage,
nor prowess; out of delusion, she slays even a serpent that is not venomous.
A woman whose qualities of discipline have been impaired is in every way like a non-venomous snake, like food containing poison, like a king, and like a sage. 7.3.6.
Women overcome those who possess the quality of disciplined conduct but have lost their discipline; they treat with contempt one who is humble through virtue but lacks discernment regarding virtues.
They approach with wealth and such out of hope, yet they avoid one who is impoverished out of contempt. (7.3.7)
Consider how the noble sage Gautama, despite his fierce austerities, was abandoned by Ahalyā;
remember how Udayana was struck down from his palace chariot by Vāsavadattā;
and reflect on Śambara, who was forsaken by the woman he cherished because she held fast to her own body.
Indeed, a woman who is excessively pampered becomes, like a female serpent in its own home, a cause for destruction.
That they cross the waters of the ocean, having cast off the fear of death; that they enter the front of battle accompanied by horses, elephants, and chariots;
and that those born of noble lineage become wretched, falling under the power of others—[all this is for the sake of wealth].
Against that, women of ignoble mind strike out in this world. (7.3.9)
Like lightning in the sky, exceedingly flickering in its course;
like a mountain river, full of many kinds of dangers;
and like a forest, both fearful and extremely dense.
Abandon this woman, as one would abandon a meal containing poison.
They first perform pleasing acts as long as they do not know that a man is attached; but once they know him to be bound by the noose of passion, [they abandon him].
They pull them out like a fish that has swallowed bait. || 7.3.11 ||
In the evening, courtesans become like one's own body,
delightful with their flowing conversation; thereafter, at midnight, they attain a state of indifference.
Then at dawn, they abandon it like a blade of grass. || 7.3.12 ||
An *atimuktaka* creeper, having entwined [itself], has flown upward— [and so forth].
Thus is the heart of a woman, the force of river water, and the peril of the Vindhya forest.
Fickle as a lotus petal trembling in the wind, it does not remain fixed in one place.
Yet they do not take account of physical beauty,
nor sovereignty, nor noble lineage, nor learning;
among all natural dispositions, with the exception of the king of the wheel.
Who has not been brushed away by the dust from the feet of women?
One should not place trust in these women, who destroy the lineages of their husbands' families;
for they were created solely for the purpose of annihilating two families.
That which carries these [elements], and from which they arise. || 7.3.15 ||
It is a whirlpool for those who take refuge [in it], an abode of immodesty, a port for rash acts,
a storehouse of vices, a field consisting of a hundred deceptions, and a domain of mistrust; it is a casket of all illusions, difficult to grasp even by the great bulls among men.
By whom was this female machine created in the world—a poison consisting of nectar—for the destruction of the world? 7.3.16

The heart is difficult to grasp, and likewise the face is like that which is reflected within a mirror; the disposition of women is as treacherous as a mountain path through a difficult pass, and it cannot be understood.
Their mind is as fickle as water on a lotus leaf; it does not remain fixed in one place.
Women are indeed like poisonous sprouts—creepers that grow together with faults.
O Mother, [we were] raised together until the sky,
appearing as if inlaid with split sapphires, shone with the luster of blue garments; and until the sun, its rays resembling the brilliance of refined gold, blazed in the heavens.
As long as the moon, garlanded with stars, traverses the earth following the sky with its rays,
so long may this teaching of the Lord of Sages, which brings benefit to the three worlds, blaze forth.
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether dwelling on the earth or in the atmosphere,
may they always maintain loving-kindness toward all creatures.
And let them practice the Dharma by day and by night. || 7.3.19 ||
May those gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
kiṃnaras, and humans who have come here to hear the Dharma protect this world and the teaching of the Jina.
And let them always practice the Dharma taught by the Lord of Munis.
